papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Bats and their ectoparasites form complex host-vector systems capable of maintaining diverse bacterial pathogens, yet these interactions remain poorly characterized in the Caucasus. We conducted the first high-throughput molecular survey of bacterial and protozoan pathogens in bat ectoparasites in Armenia. A total of 450 ectoparasites (mites and ticks) collected from 72 bats were pooled into 189 samples and screened using microfluidic real-time PCR targeting 43 bacterial and protozoan pathogens. The ectoparasite community was dominated by Spinturnix myoti and S. psi, which showed structured but overlapping associations with Myotis blythii and Miniopterus pallidus. Bartonella DNA was detected in 34.4% of pools, whereas Rickettsia spp. was rare (1.1%). At the bat level, 62.5% of individuals carried Bartonella-positive ectoparasites. Bartonella detection frequency in pools varied significantly among ectoparasite taxa, with Spinturnix mites showing approximately higher odds of Bartonella DNA detection than Macronyssus granulosus. Life stage was a strong predictor of DNA detection, with adult mites far more frequently positive than immature stages. Host species, region, and sex did not significantly influence pool positivity. These findings highlight the potentially relevant association of spinturnicid mites in Bartonella circulation within Armenian bat colonies requiring further study and provide essential baseline data for understanding the ecology of vector-borne bacteria in the Transcaucasia.

papers.title: Coinfection patterns and associations of tick-borne pathogens in natural foci of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome: A One Health approach.
papers.abstract: Tick-borne pathogens (TBPs) circulate in complex ecological systems involving vectors, animal hosts, and humans. Coinfections have been shown to influence clinical outcomes and may complicate pathogen associations, yet current research remains limited. We adopted a One Health approach in Taizhou City, a severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) endemic area, by collecting 485 community residents, 90 confirmed SFTS patients, 1081 ticks, and 471 small mammals. Five TBPs, including Anaplasma spp., Bartonella spp., Coxiella spp., Ehrlichia spp., and spotted fever group rickettsiae (SFGR), were detected using indirect immunofluorescence assay or polymerase chain reaction. We subsequently analyzed pathogen prevalence and coinfection patterns, assessed pathogen-pathogen associations, and evaluated cross-host correlations at the township level. All five TBPs were detected across ticks, small mammals, and humans, with prevalence varying substantially. Human IgG showed diverse co-seropositivity, while coinfections in ticks and small mammals were limited. Significant pathogen-pathogen associations were observed: Anaplasma spp./Ehrlichia spp. and Ehrlichia spp./SFGR in humans, and Anaplasma spp./Coxiella spp. in small mammals. Cross-host correlations included positive associations of SFGR in ticks with community residents, Bartonella spp. in small mammals with community residents, and significant links of Anaplasma spp./Ehrlichia spp. and Anaplasma spp./SFGR between ticks and community residents. Multiple TBPs co-circulate in this SFTS epidemic area, following distinct exposure routes involving ticks and small mammals. Anaplasma spp., Ehrlichia spp., and SFGR are tick-borne, while Bartonella spp. is more associated with small mammals. IgG co-seropositivity in humans likely reflects repeated or long-term exposures rather than a single tick bite. These findings suggest that effective prevention should consider human activity patterns and the role of small mammals in sustaining pathogen circulation, while a One Health approach integrating humans, animals, and vectors can guide the development of more targeted control strategies.

papers.title: Urbanicity and Lyme Disease: 20 Year Trends in Incidence and Case Burden in the United States.
papers.abstract: Incidence of Lyme disease (LD) has increased over the last few decades in the United States (US). We examined trends in LD incidence and case burden in high-incidence jurisdictions in the US from 2000 to 2021 by urbanicity. County-level counts of confirmed LD cases from 2000 to 2021 were obtained from national surveillance data. Incidence rates were calculated using census population projections. Urbanicity was categorized using Rural-Urban Continuum Codes (RUCC). Mixed effects models were used to analyze annual changes in LD incidence. Over 70% of LD cases each year were residents of metro counties. All RUCCs had an incidence greater than 10 LD cases per 100,000 per year from 2001 to 2021. LD incidence significantly increased across all RUCCs, with the largest estimated increases in counties in moderately urban areas. Urban populations have substantially contributed to the overall burden of LD in the US, whereas populations in more moderately urban areas had the largest estimated increases in LD incidence. These findings highlight the need for targeted educational interventions and public health measures across urbanicity levels to address the rising burden of LD in the US.

papers.title: Things We Do for No Reason-Polymerase Chain Reaction for Lyme Disease Diagnostic Testing.
papers.abstract: Borrelia burgdorferi polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing demonstrated a low positivity rate of 1.9% (17/885), minimal impact on clinical decision-making, and considerable healthcare cost expenditures in a Lyme disease endemic area. These findings reinforce adherence to guideline-recommended serologic testing and support diagnostic stewardship initiatives to limit unnecessary PCR utilization.

papers.title: A New Outlook on Infection-Associated Chronic Conditions and Illnesses.
papers.abstract: Infection-associated chronic conditions and illnesses (IACCI) encompass several debilitating syndromes with overlapping symptoms that have been identified and documented for decades, primarily following infectious disease outbreaks. Conditions following infection that are diagnosed with objective clinical tests have been relatively well characterized and accepted by the medical establishment, although the relationship to infection can be challenging to establish. In contrast, syndromes that lack objective tests, even when following a recognized infection, such as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, and dysautonomia, are underrecognized and often stigmatized. The COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent recognition of Long COVID as the newest example of IACCI offer new opportunities to address all aspects of IACCI. Lessons learned from the government's multi-agency public health response to Long COVID could be beneficial to ensure readiness for the long-term consequences of sporadic infections, outbreaks, and future pandemics.

papers.title: Molecular surveillance of Bartonella species, Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses in wild small mammals and their associated chigger mites in South Korea.
papers.abstract: Wild small mammals are important hosts of diverse zoonotic pathogens. Molecular surveillance incorporating both small mammals and their associated ectoparasites can provide information on pathogen detection at the wildlife-ectoparasite interface. In this study, 1,444 wild small mammals and 12,869 associated chigger mites, analyzed as 680 host-associated pools, were collected from 17 sites in South Korea between 2022 and 2025. Samples were examined for Bartonella spp., Coxiella burnetii, and orthohantaviruses using PCR- and RT-PCR-based methods, followed by sequence and phylogenetic analyses. The predominant small-mammal species, Apodemus agrarius, accounted for 84.9% of captured small mammals. DNA related to Bartonella schoenbuchensis was detected in 473 of 680 chigger mite pools (69.6%), whereas DNA related to Bartonella bacilliformis, Bartonella henselae, and Bartonella taylorii was detected in three of 1,444 small-mammal liver samples (0.2%) for each taxon. DNA of Coxiella burnetii was detected in 51 of 1,444 liver samples (3.5%), all collected during the autumn 2024 survey. Orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 37 small mammals (2.6%), predominantly in A. agrarius (35/37, 94.6%), with the remaining two detections in Crocidura spp. (2/37, 5.4%), and in three chigger mite pools (0.4%). To our knowledge, these findings provide the first molecular evidence of DNA related to B. schoenbuchensis in host-associated chigger mite pools and document previously unreported DNA related to B. bacilliformis and B. henselae in wild small-mammal liver samples in South Korea. The results provide descriptive baseline data for wildlife-based molecular surveillance; they do not establish seasonal patterns, individual-mite infection prevalence, or vector competence.

papers.title: Molecular detection of Borrelia puertoricensis and a Coxiella endosymbiont in Ornithodoros puertoricensis from northern Veracruz, Mexico.
papers.abstract: Tick-borne relapsing fever (TBRF) is a neglected zoonosis caused by Borrelia spp. and transmitted by soft ticks of the genus Ornithodoros. Although Mexico has a long history of human TBRF, the current distribution of relapsing fever borreliae and their associated vectors remains poorly understood, particularly in the Mexican Gulf Coast region. This study investigated the presence of tick-borne bacteria in ticks collected at a​ veterinary clinic in northern Veracruz, Mexico. A total of 164 Ornithodoros puertoricensis ticks were identified using morphological characteristics and 16 S mitochondrial ribosomal RNA sequencing. DNA extracts were screened by conventional PCR for Borrelia, Rickettsia, Bartonella, Coxiella, and Ehrlichia/Anaplasma, followed by DNA sequencing and phylogenetic analyses of positive samples. Borrelia puertoricensis DNA was detected in six ticks (3.66%), in four nymphs and two females. Phylogenetic analyses of the flaB gene confirmed that all sequences clustered within the B. puertoricensis clade with strong bootstrap support. In addition, a Coxiella endosymbiont was detected and assigned to clade B based on 16 S rRNA phylogenetic reconstruction, representing the first molecular evidence of this lineage in O. puertoricensis. None of the DNA samples were positive for Rickettsia, Bartonella, Ehrlichia, or Anaplasma. These findings provide the first molecular evidence of B. puertoricensis and a Coxiella clade B endosymbiont in O. puertoricensis from Veracruz, extending the known distribution of both microorganisms in Mexico. The detection of these bacteria in ticks collected at a veterinary clinic capable of treating wild animals highlights the importance of integrated acarological and molecular surveillance at wildlife-domestic animal-human interfaces to improve understanding of the ecology and public health significance of neglected tick-borne zoonoses.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: The management of moderate to severe systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) has advanced considerably with the introduction of B-cell-targeted therapies. Several emerging tick-borne diseases (eTBDs) have gained increasing attention as causes of febrile illness with potentially serious complications in predominantly immunocompromised, B-cell-depleted individuals. Since the occurrence of eTBDs remains insufficiently studied in SLE, we aimed to determine whether such infections remain undetected among patients living in a tick-endemic region of Southeastern Sweden. Biobanked sera (n = 143) collected during 2015-2024 from 48 SLE patients receiving rituximab or belimumab in Region Östergötland were included. As comparators, samples from patients with quiescent disease on hydroxychloroquine treatment only (n = 50) were analysed. All samples were investigated by real-time polymerase chain reaction assays for the presence of the eTBD pathogens Neoehrlichia mikurensis, Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato, Borrelia miyamotoi, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Spiroplasma ixodetis, and Babesia spp. No pathogen-specific DNA for the examined eTBDs was detected in serum samples from the included patients. Evidence suggests that B-cell-targeted therapies may raise eTBD risk; however, none of the individuals with SLE included herein was found to be infected, despite the documented presence of these pathogens in Southeastern Sweden. Our findings contrast with those from Norwegian immunocompromised patients, but are in line with data from the Danish nationwide Rheumatological Database, including patients with arthritis receiving tumour necrosis factor inhibitors. Hypothetically, higher doses of glucocorticoids impair B-cell function and increase the risk of eTBD further. Nevertheless, routine eTBD screening of patients with SLE in Southeastern Sweden is not supported by our data.

papers.title: Nationwide molecular survey of Babesia and Theileria DNA in wild rodents and mites collected from rodents in Korea.
papers.abstract: Piroplasm parasites of the genera Babesia and Theileria are widely distributed in wildlife and are maintained through complex host-vector transmission systems. Rodents play important roles as reservoir hosts for various arthropod-borne pathogens; however, comparative investigations integrating multiple host compartments and host-associated ectoparasites remain limited. In this study, we conducted a nationwide molecular survey of Babesia and Theileria species in wild rodents and mites collected from rodents in Korea. Rodent blood and liver tissues, together with mite pools, were examined using PCR-based detection methods, and spatial and seasonal variation in pathogen detection patterns was evaluated. Babesia microti was detected in both rodent blood and liver tissues, with higher positivity in blood and marked spatial and seasonal heterogeneity. The higher positivity observed in blood was consistent with the intraerythrocytic biology of B. microti, although differences in analytical sensitivity between sample types were not evaluated. Theileria capreoli DNA was detected exclusively at low frequency in mite pools, whereas Theileria luwenshuni DNA was detected at low frequency in both rodents and mite pools. Because mites are not established biological vectors of these Theileria species, detections in mite pools were interpreted as molecular occurrence rather than evidence of transmission or vector competence. Significant regional and seasonal variation was observed in blood and mite samples; however, overall detection frequencies were low, warranting cautious ecological interpretation. This nationwide, multi-compartment assessment highlights the ecological complexity of piroplasm circulation in wildlife systems and underscores the importance of integrated surveillance approaches when interpreting parasite DNA detection in arthropod assemblages.

papers.title: Molecular detection of selected tick-borne agents and genetic diversity of Theileria parva in African buffaloes from Mozambique.
papers.abstract: The African buffalo (Syncerus caffer) is an important reservoir of tick-borne pathogens and may contribute to pathogen transmission at wildlife-livestock interfaces. This study investigated the occurrence of Ehrlichia spp., Coxiella burnetii, Babesia spp., Theileria parva and the Theileria orientalis complex in 87 African buffaloes from the Marromeu Reserve, Mozambique, using molecular assays. In addition, the genetic diversity of T. parva was assessed based on distinct molecular markers. Theileria parva DNA was detected in 35/87 (40.2%) samples. Novel p104 and p67 haplotypes not previously reported in African buffaloes or cattle were detected among the sampled animals. The detected p67 sequences were distributed among groups 1, 2, and 3, encompassing different allele types. No sample was positive for Ehrlichia spp., E. ruminantium, T. orientalis complex, Babesia bigemina, Babesia bovis, or C. burnetii. These findings demonstrate a high molecular occurrence and substantial genetic diversity of T. parva, reinforcing the role of African buffaloes as key reservoirs of the causative agent of Corridor Disease.
papers.journal: Revista brasileira de parasitologia veterinaria = Brazilian journal of veterinary parasitology : Orgao Oficial do Colegio Brasileiro de Parasitologia Veterinaria

papers.title: A Case Report of Meningitis due to Borrelia Species in Arizona.
papers.abstract: Lyme disease is most prevalent in the Northeast and Midwest regions of the United States, as well as northern California; however, cases have been reported in nonendemic areas, including the Southwestern United States. Atypical presentations or underreporting can cause delay in diagnosis. We present the case of a 22-year-old previously healthy man, who presented to our emergency department in metropolitan Phoenix with five days of headache, fever, meningismus, and photophobia, and later developed focal neurologic deficits consistent with Lyme meningitis. Cerebrospinal fluid was notable for lymphocytic pleocytosis, and Western blot for Borrelia burgdorferi Immunoglobulin-M antibodies was positive, which led us to Lyme meningitis as the unifying diagnosis. He was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and his symptoms resolved. This case highlights the importance of considering this pathology in nonendemic areas.
papers.journal: Clinical practice and cases in emergency medicine

papers.title: Cardiovascular Manifestations of Lyme Disease.
papers.abstract: Lyme disease is a tick-borne zoonosis caused by Borrelia burgdorferi that can involve multiple organ systems, including the cardiovascular (CV) system, noted in ~1-10% of untreated patients. This can produce atrioventricular (AV) or bundle branch block, atrial fibrillation, and myopericarditis in the acute phase, and dilated cardiomyopathy in the chronic phase. Myocardial involvement may lead to ventricular tachyarrhythmias and sudden death. AV block is reported in ~90% of cases, and in 30-60% of cases, it may necessitate cardiac pacing, at least temporarily, as most cases of high-degree AV blocks resolve with antibiotic therapy within 1 week. Occasionally, aortic dissection may occur. Although Lyme carditis, in the form of myocarditis, pericarditis, and less often endocarditis, is generally self-limited with early appropriate therapy, there is also the potential for lasting CV sequelae, such as persistent AV block (noted in 90% of cases), dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure, and the rare occurrence of coronary artery involvement and aneurysmal changes. Patients with Lyme disease should receive oral tetracycline or penicillin, which can decrease the incidence of late-stage disease; however, some patients may fail early treatment. In cases of aseptic meningitis and radiculoneuritis, IV penicillin will be needed. As Lyme disease has now replaced syphilis as the "Great Imitator," physicians should be at vigilance for the disease, especially in endemic areas, and be familiarized with the particular skin rash of erythema chronicum migrans, an expanding skin lesion with the characteristic "bull's-eye" appearance patch with a center of clear skin and a distinct peripheral outer erythematous ring.

papers.title: Possible post-infectious sequelae of tick-borne Rickettsia and Ehrlichia infections.
papers.abstract: To assess the presence of symptoms and immunological profiles after infection with tick-borne spotted fever rickettsiosis (SFR) or ehrlichiosis. Adults evaluated for acute tick-borne disease completed symptom surveys through 90 days. Cases were classified using standard epidemiological definitions. Participants with alpha-gal sensitization were excluded from the primary analysis. Acute and convalescent cytokine profiles were compared between participants with and without symptoms present at the 90-day timepoint. Among 71 participants, 37 (52.1%) and 33 (46.5%) met criteria for confirmed or probable ehrlichiosis and SFR, respectively; seven met criteria for both. After excluding 12 participants with alpha-gal sensitization, 15 (50.0%) with ehrlichiosis and 13 (50.0%) with SFR reported at least one moderate or severe symptom at 90 days, compared with one of eight (12.5%) participants classified as not a case. Fatigue and musculoskeletal pain were most common. Participants with symptoms present at 90-days showed higher pro-inflammatory and lower anti-inflammatory cytokine levels, but differences were not statistically significant. Post-infectious syndromes after tick-borne disease may not be limited to Lyme disease. These preliminary findings support patient-reported experiences and warrant larger studies to define the prevalence, predictors, pathogenesis, and clinical course of possible persistent symptoms.
papers.journal: International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases

papers.title: Iron sourcing strategies and adaptive protein responses to iron deprivation in the intraerythrocytic parasite Babesia divergens.
papers.abstract: Iron is indispensable for the survival and pathogenicity of Babesia parasites, yet the mechanisms underlying its acquisition remain largely unresolved. In contrast to other apicomplexan parasites, tick-borne Babesia species rapidly lose the parasitophorous vacuole following erythrocyte invasion and do not form hemozoin, suggesting the evolution of distinct strategies for iron metabolism. Here, we demonstrate that Babesia divergens utilizes a sequential, multi-route iron acquisition system to meet its metabolic demands within host erythrocytes. Kinetic uptake analyses reveal a pronounced preference for ferrous iron (Fe2+), which is imported through an active, energy-dependent process supported by extracellular ferric reductase activity that converts host-derived ferric iron (Fe3+) into a bioavailable form prior to uptake. Using immunogold transmission electron microscopy, we provide evidence for the active internalization of host transferrin and show that parasite proliferation is dose-dependently inhibited by apo-transferrin, establishing iron as a limiting factor for parasite growth. Quantitative proteomic profiling revealed a limited, stage-specific response to deferoxamine-induced iron deprivation. Three proteins showed statistically significant changes in abundance in free merozoites: the conserved multipass membrane protein Bdiv_019230 increased, whereas the hypothetical protein Bdiv_002300 and the putative serine hydroxymethyltransferase Bdiv_027330 decreased. No proteins reached the statistical significance threshold in intraerythrocytic parasites. These results identify a small set of statistically supported candidates for investigating the response of extracellular B. divergens merozoites to iron-restricted conditions.

papers.title: Detection of vector-borne organisms in domestic cats in the United States and Canada (2019 - 2025) with analysis of Hepatozoon variants.
papers.abstract: Published large-scale vector-borne organism (VBO) PCR prevalence studies in domestic cats are limited. The prevalence of VBOs in feline blood samples submitted for PCR testing by a veterinary diagnostic laboratory between January 2, 2019, and December 23, 2025 (n = 7581) was determined. Feline blood samples were tested for Anaplasma, Apicomplexa, Babesia, Bartonella, Cytauxzoon, Ehrlichia, hemotropic Mycoplasma, and Rickettsia. VBOs were detected in 1373/7581 (18.1%) blood samples, with Mycoplasma haemominutum (8.87%) and Bartonella henselae (5.99%) being the most prevalent. Hepatozoon spp. were identified in 40 (0.58%) cats, prompting further genetic and epidemiologic characterization. Sequence analysis of a 182-bp fragment of the Hepatozoon 18S rRNA gene from 40 PCR-positive cats identified seven haplotypes with the highest sequence similarities to Hepatozoon silvestris, Hepatozoon felis, and bobcat-associated Hepatozoon spp. Phylogenetic analysis resolved the variants into major groups clustering with H. silvestris, H. felis, and nondomestic felid-associated Hepatozoon spp. Most Hepatozoon-positive cats originated from the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic regions of the United States (34/40; 85.0%), of which seven infections (7/40; 17.5%) involved cats undergoing blood donor screening. Overall, PCR testing confirmed infection with a VBO in approximately one in five cats tested in the U.S and Canada. Hepatozoon infections were more common than previously recognized, underscoring the value of Hepatozoon-specific PCR in feline VBO diagnostic testing.

papers.title: Babesia blood donor screening: A tool for safety and surveillance.
papers.abstract: Babesia is a transfusion-transmissible, tick-borne parasite endemic in the northeastern and upper midwestern US. Since 2020, nucleic acid test screening of blood donations has been implemented in endemic areas to reduce transfusion-transmitted babesiosis. American Red Cross blood donations collected between May 2020 and April 2026 in 13 endemic states and Washington, DC, were screened using the FDA-licensed Procleix Babesia transcription-mediated amplification assay. Reactive donations were analyzed by season, geography, donor characteristics, and state-level reactivity rates. Incidence estimates were evaluated using rolling 2-year periods. About 10 million donations were screened, of which 2505 were Babesia-reactive. Overall donor reactivity increased significantly from 0.02% during 2020-2021 to 0.03% during 2021-2026 (p < .001). Significant increases were observed in Maine, New York, and Pennsylvania, and no state demonstrated a significant decline. Donation reactivity exhibited a consistent seasonal pattern, while geographic analyses showed expansion of donor reactivity across the northeastern US, particularly along the eastern seaboard. Incidence increased from 63.2 to 71.0 per 100,000 person-years across the study period, with sustained increases in several states. Among 1638 reinstated donors, 59% returned to donate and 2% tested reactive again, suggesting persistent infection or reinfection. Six years of routine Babesia screening have effectively protected the blood supply while providing valuable surveillance for asymptomatic infection. Rising donor reactivity, expanding geographic distribution, and evidence of persistent or recurrent infection indicate an increasing risk of babesiosis in the United States and support continued screening and surveillance.

papers.title: One Health approach to Babesia and Bartonella species: occupational zoonotic infections in veterinary workers and their families.
papers.abstract: This study investigated the presence of Babesia, Bartonella, and Borrelia spp infection in an extended veterinary family. Between May 2023 and August 2025, 8 individuals enrolled in an Institutional Review Board-approved observational study. Serological evidence of Bartonella spp exposure and molecular evidence of Babesia, Bartonella, and Borrelia spp infection were assessed. Among other symptoms, at least half of the study participants reported chronic fatigue, headaches, anxiety, depression, and difficulty remembering. On the basis of PCR amplification and DNA sequencing, infection with Babesia odocoilei, Babesia divergens-like MO-1, Babesia gibsoni, or Babesia microti was confirmed in 4 individuals. Three other individuals were PCR positive for Piroplasmida/Apicomplexa DNA. Four individuals were seroreactive to 1 or more Bartonella spp and 6 individuals were Bartonella PCR positive in blood, serum, or enrichment blood cultures. Six individuals had at least 1 Borrelia partition detected by digital PCR; however, efforts in our laboratory to confirm Borrelia digital PCR positivity by DNA sequencing were not successful. Similar to this extended veterinary family, previous studies have documented that veterinarians and veterinary workers may be occupationally at risk for exposure to Bartonella spp. On the basis of the results of this study, veterinary workers may also be at risk for infection with Babesia spp and potentially other Piroplasmida/Apicomplexa organisms. The potential that chronic intravascular or endotheliotropic infections with vector-borne pathogens contributes to multisystem illnesses in veterinary workers deserves future research considerations, which, on a clinical, epidemiological, and microbiological basis, will require sequential lifetime studies.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association

papers.title: Bacterial diversity associated with Streblidae flies parasitizing cave-dwelling bats from northeastern Brazil.
papers.abstract: Bats (Chiroptera) are highly diverse mammals that play key ecological roles and harbor a wide range of microorganisms, yet the microbiome of their ectoparasitic flies remains poorly understood. This study characterized and compared the bacterial microbiomes associated with two bat-ectoparasite systems, Pteronotus gymnonotus-Trichobius johnsonae and Desmodus rotundus-Trichobius parasiticus, from cave-dwelling bat populations in northeastern Brazil using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Sixty-eight bat fly samples were successfully sequenced, and 67 were retained for downstream ecological analyses after quality filtering. Bacterial communities were dominated by members of the classes Gammaproteobacteria and Alphaproteobacteria, with Arsenophonus, Bartonella, and unresolved endosymbiont-associated taxa among the most abundant bacterial groups. Alpha-diversity patterns varied according to the metric considered: observed ASV richness was influenced by bat fly species, sex, and their interaction, Shannon diversity differed according to streblid fly species and sex, and Faith's phylogenetic diversity differed between bat fly sexes. Notably, male T. johnsonae exhibited greater observed ASV richness than females, whereas no significant sex difference was detected in T. parasiticus. Beta-diversity analyses consistently revealed differences in bacterial community composition between the two bat-ectoparasite systems, while the influence of sex was system-dependent, with significant differentiation between T. johnsonae males and females but not between sexes of T. parasiticus in phylogenetically informed analyses. Differential abundance analysis further identified Romboutsia, Bartonella, Bacteroides, and an unclassified Pseudomonadota genus as discriminatory taxa among groups. Overall, these findings reveal distinct bacterial diversity and composition patterns between the two bat-ectoparasite systems and indicate that sex-associated microbiome variation is not uniform across bat fly species.
papers.journal: Comparative immunology, microbiology and infectious diseases

papers.title: Diversity and distribution of Bartonella spp. in domestic animals, wildlife, and ectoparasites in Brazil: a comprehensive review.
papers.abstract: Bartonella are intracellular Gram-negative blood-borne bacteria capable of infecting a wide range of hosts, primarily mammals and birds. They are responsible for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases characterized by persistent intraerythrocytic bacteremia in mammals. Out of 49 species described, 13 presents zoonotic potential. This review aimed to update the current knowledge on the occurrence, distribution, and genetic diversity of Bartonella in domestic animals, wild mammals and birds, and ectoparasites in Brazil. A total of 72 scientific articles published between 2007 and 2026 were included. The available information indicates that the Southeastern and Central-Western regions of Brazil account for most reports of Bartonella in animals and ectoparasites, whereas the Northern and Northeastern regions remain comparatively understudied. Overall, studies investigating Bartonella in Brazil have become increasingly frequent and geographically widespread over the years. Although some investigations rely on single-gene analyses, most employ multi-locus sequence analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction, providing stronger evidence for species identification and diversity. In contrast, relatively few studies have incorporated whole-genome sequencing or comprehensive phenotypic and biochemical characterization through bacterial isolation and blood culture. Future research should prioritize advanced genomic approaches and bacterial isolation to improve our understanding of the diversity, evolution, and epidemiology of Bartonella circulating in Brazil.
papers.journal: Revista brasileira de parasitologia veterinaria = Brazilian journal of veterinary parasitology : Orgao Oficial do Colegio Brasileiro de Parasitologia Veterinaria

papers.title: Ecological niche partitioning and urbanization-driven restructuring of flea-borne pathogen communities in stray carnivores of Peninsular Malaysia: discovery of uncharacterised Bartonella lineages.
papers.abstract: Flea-borne bacteria are emerging zoonotic pathogens of increasing public health importance, yet their ecological distribution, community structure, and genetic diversity across contrasting landscapes in Southeast Asia remain poorly understood. This study investigated flea infestation, flea-borne bacterial pathogens, and their ecological associations in stray cats and dogs across urban, peri-urban, and rural landscapes of Peninsular Malaysia. A total of 296 stray cats and dogs were examined for flea infestation, and all recovered fleas (n = 636) were identified morphologically and screened individually for Bartonella spp., Rickettsia spp., and Orientia tsutsugamushi using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays followed by Sanger sequencing and phylogenetic analysis. Risk factors associated with flea infestation, Bartonella spp. and Rickettsia spp. occurrence were evaluated using generalized linear models (GLMs), generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs), and Firth's penalized logistic regression, respectively. Pathogen community structure was assessed using alpha diversity indices, non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS), permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), and tripartite ecological network analysis. Overall flea infestation prevalence was 32.09% (95/296), with infestation significantly higher in cats (39.44%) than dogs (13.25%) (χ2 = 10.672, df = 1, p = 0.001). All 636 fleas exhibited complete host-associated segregation, with Ctenocephalides felis (n = 485) occurring exclusively on cats and C. orientis (n = 151) exclusively on dogs. Flea-borne pathogens were detected in 71.86% (457/636) of fleas, comprising Bartonella henselae, B. clarridgeiae, B. koehlerae, several uncharacterized Bartonella lineages, Rickettsia felis, and R. asembonensis. Urban landscapes were associated with significantly higher Bartonella prevalence in C. felis (70.05%), whereas C. orientis was overwhelmingly dominated by R. asembonensis (94.04%). Ecological analyses demonstrated significant landscape-associated variation in pathogen community composition among C. felis populations but not C. orientis. Phylogenetic analysis identified a distinct, well-supported clade of previously uncharacterized Bartonella lineages (bootstrap = 100%). No O. tsutsugamushi was detected in any flea sample. Flea-borne pathogen communities in Peninsular Malaysia are structured by strong host-vector associations and ecological landscape, with peri-urban environments supporting greater pathogen diversity and urban landscapes demonstrated higher detection of Bartonella in C. felis. The discovery of previously uncharacterized Bartonella lineages expands the known diversity of flea-associated Bartonella in Malaysia and highlights the importance of integrating molecular epidemiology with community ecology to improve surveillance of emerging flea-borne zoonoses.

papers.abstract: The Lyme disease spirochete Borreliella burgdorferi possesses bipolar periplasmic flagella that are essential for its distinctive flat-wave morphology, motility, and infectivity. However, how the molecular architecture of these flagella contributes to spirochetal morphology and motility remains poorly understood. Here, using in situ single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, we determine near-atomic structures of native periplasmic flagellar filaments and reveal two distinct architectures: half-sheathed and unsheathed. We show that the spirochete-specific protein FlaA forms an asymmetric sheath along the convex surface of the conserved FlaB filament core, with sheath assembly restricted to the proximal filament region near the flagellar motor. Atomic models reveal that FlaA anchors to the FlaB core through specific interactions with two surface-exposed loops, while genetic and motility analyses demonstrate distinct roles for these loops in maintaining cell morphology and motility. Structural comparisons reveal that the FlaB core possesses intrinsic curvature and supercoiling, which are substantially amplified by asymmetric FlaA assembly. These findings support a model in which localized FlaA sheath assembly reinforces the proximal filament and potentially modulates its mechanical properties. Together, our results uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism by which asymmetric sheath assembly enhances flagellar supercoiling, providing a molecular basis for understanding the distinctive morphology and motility of spirochetes. The Lyme disease spirochete Borreliella burgdorferi relies on periplasmic flagella for its distinctive morphology and motility, but how filament architecture contributes to these properties remains unclear. Using in situ cryo-electron microscopy, we reveal that the spirochete-specific protein FlaA forms an asymmetric sheath around the FlaB filament core exclusively near the cell poles. FlaA anchors to flexible surface loops of FlaB through specific molecular interactions, while genetic analyses reveal distinct roles for these loops in maintaining cell morphology and motility. Asymmetric FlaA assembly amplifies the intrinsic supercoiling of the FlaB core, potentially modifying filament mechanics near the motor. These findings reveal how localized, asymmetric sheath assembly contributes to the distinctive morphology and motility of spirochetes.

papers.abstract: Hepatosplenic cat-scratch disease (HS-CSD) is a rare manifestation of Bartonella henselae infection in immunocompetent adults and may closely mimic haematological malignancy. A 62-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with an eight-week history of fever, night sweats and weight loss. A fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography-computed tomography (FDG PET/CT) revealed hypermetabolic hepatosplenic lesions, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and a focal acetabular bone lesion, strongly suggesting stage IV lymphoma or metastatic disease. Bone marrow biopsy showed no evidence of malignancy; liver biopsy revealed caseous necrotising granulomas. Mycobacterial polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and cultures were negative. Bartonella serology demonstrated a high IgG titre (>1:1.280), while tissue PCR was borderline positive. Treatment with azithromycin and rifampicin for four weeks resulted in clinical improvement and resolution of constitutional symptoms. HS-CSD can closely mimic advanced malignancy. In patients with prolonged fever, visceral lesions and feline exposure, B. henselae infection should be considered early in the diagnostic workup. HS-CSD may closely mimic advanced malignancy.Feline exposure should prompt consideration of Bartonella henselae infection in patients with prolonged fever and visceral lesions, to avoid unnecessary investigations or inappropriate treatments.

papers.title: A molecular clutch governs stator engagement and flagellar torque.
papers.abstract: Motile bacteria must continuously adjust their motility to navigate and colonize diverse environments, including mammalian hosts, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, using in situ single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, we determine near-atomic structures of the flagellar motor in the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi and uncover a novel mechanism for controlling torque generation. We identify a distinct neutral state in which individual torque-generating MotA 5 B 2 stator complexes remain incorporated in the motor but adopt an extended, tilted conformation disengaged from the rotor. Two conserved flagellar proteins, FliL and FlcA, form a transmembrane scaffold that retains 16 stator complexes, while FapA, a newly identified multidomain flagellar protein, binds the cytoplasmic base of the stator complex and stabilizes its rotor-disengaged conformation. Strikingly, rotor-engaged and rotor-disengaged stators coexist within individual motors, demonstrating that stator retention and torque engagement are separable states. Our findings establish a motor-retained neutral stator state and reveal a molecular-clutch mechanism that independently controls the engagement of individual stator units with the rotor, enabling rapid and precise regulation of flagellar torque and motility.

papers.abstract: Bacterial flagellar motors are diverse rotary machines that require robust mechanical coupling to transmit torque across components with distinct architectures, yet how such coupling is achieved remains poorly understood. Here, we determine near-atomic in situ structures of the periplasmic flagellar motor in the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi , revealing how an expanded rotor is mechanically coupled to the conserved rod through symmetry breaking and local remodeling of the rotor-rod interface. Surprisingly, pentameric FrbA forms a split washer-shaped brace around the rotor-rod junction, providing a second layer of mechanical reinforcement. Deletion of frbA destabilizes distal flagellar structures and impairs motility, particularly under increased viscous load. FrbA homologues are broadly distributed across spirochetes, suggesting a conserved mechanism for reinforcing high-torque flagellar motors. Together, these findings reveal how symmetry breaking couples an expanded rotor to a conserved driveshaft, while a molecular split washer reinforces this interface to enable robust torque transmission and motility.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Accurate diagnosis of Lyme disease remains challenging as early clinical manifestations are often nonspecific and erythema migrans lesions are not always present, necessitating reliable serological testing. In this study, we aimed to compare the agreements of various simulated serological standard two-tier testing (STTT) and modified two-tier testing (MTTT) algorithms, with particular focus on identifying trends and potential redundancies between assay configurations. A total of 342 patient serum samples were collected between 2021 and 2024 and subjected to testing using various kits. Evaluated enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) included ZEUS (VlsE1/pepC10 IgG/IgM, Whole-Cell IgG/IgM, IgG, and IgM) and DiaSorin LIAISON (Total Antibody Plus, IgG, and IgM). Immunoblots included Mikrogen IgG/IgM and Euroimmun IgG/IgM assays targeting Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato. Twelve MTTT algorithms and six STTT algorithms were evaluated. Overall percentage agreements were calculated between algorithms to assess concordance in the final serological classification. Overall seroreactivity varied by algorithm. Although one STTT algorithm yielded the greatest number of interpreted positives, MTTT algorithms on average yielded a greater number of samples interpreted as positive (165/342, 48.2%, 95% CI 43.0% to 53.5%) compared with the STTT algorithms (148/342, 43.3%, 95% CI 38.0% to 48.5%). The highest overall percentage agreements (>95%) among MTTT algorithms were only observed when both algorithms employed the same EIAs detecting combined IgG/IgM antibodies, but applied in reverse order (ie, first- and second-tier tests interchanged). MTTT algorithms demonstrated higher and more consistent positivity rates than STTT algorithms, although this should not be interpreted as evidence of superior accuracy in the absence of a reference standard. Concerningly, certain configurations of MTTTs showed high agreement with one another, likely attributable to shared antigen targets. These findings underscore the need for careful validation of assay combinations to avoid redundancy and optimize harmonized Lyme disease diagnostic strategies in Canada. Il est difficile de bien diagnostiquer la maladie de Lyme. En effet, les premières manifestations cliniques sont non spécifiques et les lésions d’érythème migrateur ne sont pas toujours présentes, ce qui entraîne le recours à une épreuve sérologique fiable. Dans la présente étude, les auteurs ont cherché à comparer les divers algorithmes de sérologie à deux volets standards (SDVS) et de sérologie à deux volets modifiés (SDVM), tout particulièrement les tendances et les redondances potentielles entre les deux configurations. Au total, 342 échantillons de sérum de patients ont été prélevés entre 2021 et 2024 et soumis à des tests à l'aide de diverses trousses. Les épreuves immunoenzymatiques évaluées incluaient la solution ZEUS (IgG/IgM, IgG/IgM VlsE1/pepC10, IgG et IgM entières) et la solution LIAISON de DiaSorin (IgG et IgM des anticorps totaux plus). Les immunotransferts incluaient les épreuves IgG/IgM Mikrogen et les épreuves IgG/IgM Euroimmun qui ciblaient les bactéries Borrelia burgdorferi au sens large. Douze algorithmes de SDVM et six algorithmes de SDVS ont été évalués. Dans l'ensemble, leurs corrélations globales ont été calculées en pourcentage pour évaluer la concordance de la classification sérologique définitive. Dans l'ensemble, la séroréactivité variait selon l'algorithme. Même si un algorithme de SDVS produisait le plus d'interprétations de résultats positifs, les algorithmes de SDVM, en moyenne, produisaient plus d’échantillons interprétés comme positifs (165 sur 342, 48,2 %, IC à 95 % : 43,0 % à 53,5 %) que les algorithmes de SDVS (148 sur 342, 43,3 %, IC à 95 % : 38,0 % à 48,5 %). Les corrélations globales calculées en pourcentage des algorithmes de SDVM les plus élevées (>95 %) ont été observées seulement lorsque les deux algorithmes faisaient appel aux mêmes épreuves immunoenzymatiques qui détectaient des anticorps aux IgG/IgM combinées, mais appliquées à rebours (c'est-à-dire que les premier et deuxième volets étaient inversés). Les algorithmes de SDVM ont obtenu des taux de résultats positifs plus élevés et plus constants que les algorithmes de SDVS, mais en l'absence de norme de référence, il ne faudrait pas interpréter ces observations comme des preuves d'une meilleure précision. Il est inquiétant de constater que certaines configurations de SDVM présentaient une corrélation élevée entre elles, probablement attribuables à des cibles d'antigène communes. Ces résultats soulignent la nécessité de procéder à une validation attentive des combinaisons d’épreuves pour éviter la redondance et optimiser les stratégies diagnostiques harmonisées de la maladie de Lyme au Canada.

papers.title: Retrospective Serological Survey of Equine Influenza Virus and Piroplasm Parasites in Free-Ranging Wild Equids from Kenya and Tanzania.
papers.abstract: Wild equids may act as reservoirs for infectious pathogens affecting domestic equine populations, yet data on exposure to equine infectious anemia virus (EIAV), equine influenza virus (EIV), and equine piroplasmosis agents in African wildlife remain scarce. Our objectives were to retrospectively determine serological evidence of exposure to EIAV, EIV, Theileria equi, and Babesia caballi among Grevy's zebras and rhinoceroses from Kenya and Tanzania. A total of 284 archived serum samples from 215 Grevy's zebras and 69 rhinoceroses were analyzed using commercial ELISAs. Positive EIAV screening tests were retested using a second confirmatory assay. No confirmed EIAV antibodies were detected in zebras or rhinoceroses. Antibodies against EIV were identified in 20/215 zebras (9.3%), all originating from Serengeti National Park. Theileria equi antibodies were detected in 194/206 zebras (94.2%), while Babesia caballi antibodies were detected in 8/206 zebras (3.9%). Rhinoceroses were negative for all pathogens tested. This study provides evidence of widespread exposure of Grevy's zebras to T. equi and limited exposure to EIV in East Africa while failing to identify serologic evidence of EIAV infection in zebras or rhinoceroses. These findings improve understanding of infectious disease ecology at the wildlife-livestock interface and support continued wildlife surveillance programs.

papers.title: A SAGA-like AP2-P-ARP1-GCN5 transcriptional complex targets pathogenesis-associated genes during the blood-stage development of Babesia gibsoni.
papers.abstract: Babesiosis is an increasingly recognized tick-borne zoonosis. The asexual blood stage of its causative agent, Babesia, drives pathological damages in the host and can cause severe or fatal human infections. Nevertheless, the transcriptional regulatory mechanisms that control this developmental stage remain poorly characterized. Here, we identified a novel ApiAP2 transcription factor (AP2-P; pathogenesis), which is essential in the blood-stage development of B. gibsoni. Nuclear import of AP2-P is inhibited by ivermectin, which is likely mediated via the IMPα/β pathway. Importantly, AP2-P forms a SAGA-like complex with the histone acetyltransferase GCN5 and a novel AP2-P related protein 1 (ARP1). Conditional knockdown of ARP1 or GCN5 results in reduced parasite growth rates accompanied by alterations in expression profiles and chromatin accessibility of pathogenesis-related genes. ChIP-seq data indicate that the complex associates with both euchromatic regions marked by H3K9ac and heterochromatic regions marked by H3K9me3, and it also targets many pathogenic genes by recognizing specific DNA motif, including those involved in invasion, antigenic variation, drug resistance, and sexual-stage development. Notably, normal genomic distribution pattern of AP2-P likewise depends on ARP1 or GCN5. Collectively, our study suggests a SAGA-like epigenetic module responsible for pathogenesis of Babesia gibsoni during asexual blood stage.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Theileria annulata causes tropical theileriosis in cattle and is endemic in Kazakhstan. Although molecular diagnostic methods for this pathogen exist, data on its molecular surveillance and genetic diversity in Kazakhstan remain limited. This study aimed to develop and experimentally validate a species-specific real-time PCR (qPCR) assay for the detection of Theileria annulata and to conduct molecular surveillance and phylogenetic analysis of circulating isolates. A total of 709 cattle blood samples from 10 regions of Kazakhstan were analysed. Species-specific primers and a probe were designed targeting the 18S rRNA gene, and diagnostic performance was evaluated against sequencing as the reference method. Theileria annulata infection was confirmed in 110 of 709 samples (15.51%), with positive samples identified in the Turkistan, West Kazakhstan, Kyzylorda, and Zhambyl regions. The developed assay showed high diagnostic sensitivity (99.09%), specificity (99.67%), and diagnostic efficiency (99.58%), with no cross-reactivity with Theileria orientalis, Theileria parva, Babesia bovis, Babesia bigemina, or Anaplasma marginale. Phylogenetic analysis of partial 28S rRNA sequences confirmed the species identity of the detected isolates and demonstrated their close relationship with previously reported Kazakhstani and Chinese isolates. The developed qPCR assay is suitable for the molecular diagnosis and surveillance of bovine tropical theileriosis in Kazakhstan.
